#### Introduction: five vectors of FinTech disruption Dermot Hodson a, Pierre Schlosser b and Amy Verdun c,d

aInstitute for Digital Technologies, Loughborough University, London, UK; bRobert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies, European University Institute, Florence, Italy; cDepartment of Political Science, University of Victoria, Victoria, Canada; dInstitute of Political Science, Leiden University, Leiden, Netherlands

ABSTRACT Financial Technologies (FinTech) such as mobile payments, blockchain and artificial intelligence are transforming financial services by powering faster payments and new forms of money in both developed and developing countries. FinTech is not only disrupting finance, we contend, but also contemporary politics by spurring divergent policy responses to cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and extending Big Tech’s societal reach and market power. FinTech is often presented as a catalyst for financial inclusion, but it can be a vehicle for criminality and corruption, and has intersected with the rise of right-wing populism. In this introduction, we identify five vectors of FinTech disruption covering (1) the international monetary order, (2) political authority, (3) security and trust, (4) inclusion, development and growth, and (5) financial governance. FinTech can be a force for good, but, if left unchecked, it has the potential to create a new monetary disorder.

Introduction

On 19 January 2025, the anonymous owners of two dozen digital wallets bought close to $3 million in $MELANIA crypto tokens minutes before news of the meme coin’s release was announced on X by the First Lady of the United States (US), Melania Trump (Stafford and Hammond 2025). The traders reportedly made close to $100 million by offloading most of their holdings within twelve hours (Hemingway et al. 2025). Few stories capture quite so clearly the growing political salience of financial technology (FinTech). That the First Lady of the United States could lend her name to a highly volatile crypto asset would have been unthinkable even under the First Trump Presidency. That the Second Trump Presidency has established a Bitcoin reserve and championed dollar backed stablecoins shows how rapidly the international monetary system is being disrupted. The relationship between finance and technology is not new, nor is its geopolitical sig nificance. In 1861, Western Union completed the first transcontinental cable, permitting stock tickers and wire money transfers. Six years later, the same company’s attempt to create a similar link between San Francisco and Moscow led the United States to purchase

Alaska from the Russian Empire. Fast forward 150 years, and a new wave of technological 
innovation from the rise of the smartphone and distributed ledger technologies to the 
artificial intelligence (AI) revolution is improving the speed, efficiency and coverage of 
financial services in both the Global North and the Global South. The same technologies 
are also creating new opportunities for fraudsters and cyber criminals. The political ramifi 
cations of FinTech are even more dramatic. 
The Financial Stability Board (FSB) defines FinTech as ‘technologically enabled inno 
vation in financial services that could result in new business models, applications, pro 
cesses or products with an associated material effect on financial markets and 
institutions and the provision of financial services’ (FSB 2017, p. 7). Such innovation is 
not limited to specific categories of financial service, but it has been especially prominent 
in payments, clearing and settlements, deposits, lending and capital, insurance, invest 
ment management and market support (FSB 2017, p. 8). FinTech, much like other 
forms of digital technology, is closely associated with the idea of disruption. Facebook’s 
original motto – ‘move fast and break things’ – exemplifies this idea (Taplin 2017). 
However, as Thelen (2018) notes, disruption by tech firms is as much about seeking to 
overturn existing regulation as it is about capturing incumbents’ market share (Kou 
and Lu 2025). This Special Issue goes further by arguing that FinTech is no less disruptive 
for contemporary politics. New financial technologies, we argue, are weakening public 
authorities’ grip on policy instruments ranging from monetary policy to anti-money laun 
dering controls. Some forms of FinTech are also fuelling the rise of right-wing populists, 
who have actively championed private digital currencies while opposing public alterna 
tives. Divergent domestic responses to FinTech are creating new sources of financial 
inequality, as well as addressing existing ones, and eroding traditional guardrails of 
trust and security. As a result of these changes, FinTech is dismantling key elements of 
the post-Bretton Woods system and threatening a new age of international monetary dis 
order (Strange 1990, Tavlas 1997, Cohen 2019, p. 170). 
In this introduction, we do not aim to put forward a unified theory, but rather to 
present a typology of five vectors of FinTech disruption, which can help to navigate a frag 
mented terrain for the study of international political economy. These vectors encompass 
(1) the international monetary order, (2) political authority, (3) security and trust, (4) 
inclusion, development and growth, and (5) financial governance. This list is not exhaus 
tive, but it conveys the myriad ways in which FinTech is recasting contemporary politics. 
We consider the apparent direction of each vector and warn that digital finance, for all its 
advantages, has the potential to destabilise not only financial systems but the state and 
society at large. 

Fintech: from financial to political disruption In his widely cited book, The Innovator’s Dilemma, Clayton M. Christensen (1997) distin guished between sustaining and disruptive technologies. Whereas sustaining technol ogies allow industry leaders to maintain or improve product performance, disruptive technologies redefine performance in ways that favour new entrants. From the cash machine or ATM (formally ‘Automated Teller Machine’) to telephone banking, technol ogies have historically played a sustaining role in financial services. More recent inno vations have been strongly disruptive for three reasons, however.

(i) New entrants are unconstrained by the legacy technologies which incumbents have 
built over the years and, in some cases, decades. The success of neobanks such as 
Monzo in the UK and N26 in Germany is a case in point (Bradford 2020, Mazzocchi 
and Spitzer 2026). These challenger banks have built user-friendly banking apps 
that established financial institutions have struggled to match (Hodson 2021). Simi 
larly, companies such as Revolut and Wise have disrupted the market for cross 
border payments through competitively priced alternatives to traditional inter 
national money transfers and overseas debit and credit card usage (Bindseil and Pan 
telopoulos 2022, pp. 17–8). Similar disruptions are to be noted on the online 
brokering segment as the rapid development of neo-broker Trade Republic demon 
strates (FinTech Global 2026). 
(ii) The rise of smartphones and the declining importance of bricks-and-mortar banks 
have made it easier for tech firms to diversify into financial services. A prominent 
example is Apple Pay, which has turned the iPhone into a payment device used 
by an estimated 550–600 million customers worldwide by the end of 2025 (Lee 
2025). Alipay, China’s ‘super app’, has more than a billion users worldwide (Ant 
Group 2024). 
(iii) Some forms of FinTech are highly disruptive for core banking structures and risk 
bank disintermediation (Cai 2018) because of the direct customer interface that digi 
talisation fosters. Peer-to-peer lenders such as Funding Circle and decentralised 
finance (DeFi) protocols such as Aave provide cost-effective alternatives to bank 
lending. But Lending Club’s well-documented problems in the United States and 
Ezubao’s Ponzi-style crash in China reveal the governance gaps associated with dis 
intermediation (Claessens et al. 2018). 

Christensen’s work on innovation has been criticised for ignoring the social costs of dis ruptive technologies (Kivimaa et al. 2021) and the lack of effective government regulation (Harvey et al. 2021). The costs of FinTech disruption should not be overlooked. Older financial institutions have well-developed prudential standards and compliance cultures that some start-ups struggle to emulate. Buy Now Pay Later services use alternative data sources rather than conventional credit checks to offer unsecured loans to customers who may lack the means to repay (Threadgold et al. 2025). While FinTech challengers can drive competition in banking and payments, Big FinTech companies have been accused of seeking ‘near absolute market power’ over online payments and in-app purchases (Srini vasaragavan 2025). Cryptocurrencies have been challenged, meanwhile, for their heavy consumption of energy and generation of e-waste. Bitcoin’s annual electricity usage is greater than that of some large countries (Delahaye 2024). The concept of disruption has a deeper meaning which goes beyond the impact of new technologies on specific industries. For Rile Hayward (2020), disruption is a way for subordinated actors to reshape entrenched political agendas. It is sometimes linked to techno-libertarianism, a political ideology which favours technological solutions to societal challenges in place of the state’s traditional problem-solving role (Brekke 2020). At the same time, disruption is used to describe political projects such as Brexit and Trumpism, which channel popular frustration with the status quo (Hopkin 2020). Drawing on these and other meanings of disruption, the next section enumerates the

various ways in which FinTech is impacting already-fragile power structures at the dom estic, international and transnational levels.

Five vectors of FinTech disruption 
A vector is not a point in time or space but rather an object that has magnitude and direc 
tion. In epidemiology, the term refers to organisms that carry infectious pathogens. In 
social science, the concept is used more broadly to refer to ‘patterns of social interaction 
whose repetition over time sustains or encourages further iteration’. (Gillian 2020, p. 520).
